prize_parts.citation: For the prediction of flat bands in twisted bilayer graphene at a magic angle and the experimental discovery of correlated insulating and superconducting states in this tunable moire system

statement.case_for: I keep B046 as a single achievement with Jarillo-Herrero, MacDonald and Bistritzer. The Physics Prize is for the original experiment, and here it can be named: the 2018 papers from Jarillo-Herrero's group on correlated insulator states and superconductivity at the angle that the 2011 Bistritzer-MacDonald continuum model had singled out. The prediction was quantitative and falsifiable, the experiment confirmed it in a gate-tunable device, and many groups with different probes (transport, STM, compressibility, optics) have since reproduced the flat bands and the correlated phases across several moire systems. This is a door opened onto phenomena that could not be seen or controlled before, which is what I look for in a new tool. The chair asked whether the unresolved pairing mechanism and the age of the discovery are grounds for waiting. I do not think so. The committee has repeatedly recognised the existence of a phenomenon before its explanation, and the correlated phases are not in doubt. I weighed the B028 case again and it is a strong, mature case, but the round-1 exchange has not removed my attribution doubt there, and I am more certain of the B046 chain of evidence.
statement.case_against: The honest weaknesses are three. First, the 2018 discovery is eight years old and the pairing mechanism is debated, so a sceptical member can call it early. Second, Andrei's 2010 STM work and the earlier continuum-model papers of Lopes dos Santos, Peres and Castro Neto are real precursors, and Cao and Fatemi did much of the bench work in 2018; a three-name limit leaves out real contributors and the citation and background text must say this accurately. Third, B028 and B034 are older and have fewer open questions about maturity. If the committee judged that the condensed-matter community will need another five years to settle the mechanism, B028 would be my fallback.

responses.point: Mehlig argues for B028 with Kane, Mele and Molenkamp: a simple Z2 mechanism, a prediction confirmed in HgTe, two decades of reproduction. He accepts that a slate with Hasan would be at least as defensible and that the experimental half is thin.
responses.response: I accept the maturity and the clarity of the mechanism, and I answer the chair's question on distinctness from 2016 as he does: this is band topology in real materials, not the phase-transition theory of 2016, so it is distinct. My remaining difficulty is the one he names himself. If a slate with Hasan is as defensible as one without him, and if the HgTe conductance fell short of quantisation, then the committee cannot say it is absolutely sure it has found the original experiment and the right people. For B046 the prediction and the first observation are each one identifiable paper. That is why I still place B028 second, not first, and why I would move to it if the committee cannot accept the B046 maturity argument.

responses.point: Eriksson prefers B028 and lists B046 as his first alternative. He describes B028 as a clean link between theory and measurement and notes that the credit is contested because of Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang and the 3D strand.
responses.response: We agree that both candidates leave someone out, so I do not think attribution is a tiebreaker in favour of B028. The difference I see is how many separate steps the three names must stand for. In B028 the trio leaves out a prediction that the experiment actually tested (BHZ) and a second experimental discovery (Hasan). In B046 the omissions are precursors and bench co-authors, and the decisive prediction-experiment pair is covered. I would ask him whether he accepts that, and whether his support for B046 as first alternative means he would not oppose it if B028 fails on credit.

responses.point: Danielsson proposes two parts: Halzen for IceCube and MacDonald with Jarillo-Herrero for B046. He says the three-person ceiling forces him to drop Bistritzer, and that he would revert to Jarillo-Herrero, MacDonald and Bistritzer if B046 stood alone.
responses.response: The chair asked what I would need to see before supporting a two-part prize. My answer is that the two parts must each be defensible on credit within the ceiling. The B005 part is not, in my view, since a single name for a collaboration-scale detector is open to the AMANDA, DUMAND and Baikal objections he himself lists, and the shortlist gives no further IceCube name. His B046 part would also leave out Bistritzer, who co-authored the 2011 prediction that the experiment tested. I would rather give all three seats to one achievement where the credit is complete than split them and weaken both. I welcome that he would accept B046 with three names alone, and that is my configuration.

responses.point: Kroll prefers B034 for Katori and Ye, with clean two-name attribution, reproduction across laboratories at the 10^-18 level, and the redefinition of the second pending. He asks whether the committee values measurement capability or field-opening impact.
responses.response: I like a new tool as much as anyone, and the credit for B034 is the cleanest on the shortlist. My difficulty is the one the chair put to him: what is the finding rather than the capability? Redshift over millimetres and constant searches so far set limits or confirm known physics, and the 2005 and 2012 prizes recognised the precision-measurement step. For B046 the new result is a state of matter that nobody predicted could appear in a tunable carbon device. I do not see his priority concerns (Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow and Bloom) as fatal, and I list B034 as an alternative, but I would not move it ahead of B046 unless he can name an observation that nature gave us unasked.

responses.point: Pearce prefers B028 but ranked IceCube first in his own opening. He relies on the condensed-matter members for the physics and tests the evidence chain by prediction, independent measurement and reproduction.
responses.response: I apply the same test he does, and I think B046 meets it as well: the Bistritzer-MacDonald prediction, an independent measurement in Jarillo-Herrero's group, and reproduction in several laboratories and techniques. Since he defers to us on condensed matter, I would ask him to weigh that it is the one candidate all eight members ranked in the opening, and that five of the eight list it as first alternative. I do not offer that as a substitute for the physics, which I have argued above, but it suggests a final ballot might converge on it.

uncertainties: Whether the committee accepts the unresolved pairing mechanism and an eight-year-old discovery as compatible with the prize.

Whether Bistritzer, rather than Andrei or another theorist, is the right third name, and whether the final text can credit Andrei and the earlier continuum-model theory accurately without a fourth name.
Whether B028 can be credited without leaving out Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang or Hasan, which determines whether it becomes my first choice.
My recollection of priority details in twisted bilayer graphene, topological insulators and lattice clocks is from memory and has not been verified against the record.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict with any shortlisted person. I am a Fellow of the University of Tokyo (since 2025) and have long exchanges with Japanese microscopy communities, and Katori (B034) is Tokyo-based, but I have no collaboration with him and no co-authorship with anyone credited on the shortlist. My Chalmers colleague Goran Johansson sits on the committee and now prefers B028, and I do not treat that as a reason to defer on the physics. Johansson's proposed recusal from B035 does not affect my configuration. No recusal is needed on my side.
